query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA, degradation at high temperatures in oxidizing or reducing environments is governed by a dual mechanism: (1) rapid, grain-boundary‐mediated oxygen ingress that promotes selective oxidation of the reactive elements (primarily Al and Cr) to form a layered oxide scale, and (2) the resulting microstructurally inherited discontinuities (e.g., nonuniform scale thickness or poor scale adhesion at high-angle grain boundaries) lead to scale spallation or breakdown. Under oxidizing conditions the inner protective oxide (rich in Al2O3/Cr2O3) forms inadequately continuous due to fast, localized oxidation along these boundaries, while under reducing conditions the dynamic equilibrium of oxide formation and partial reduction further destabilizes the scale.
generation.material_initial_state: As-manufactured additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an FCC matrix characterized by a refined grain structure and high grain boundary density.
generation.intervention: Conduct a controlled comparison between as-built AM samples and samples that have been post-processed (annealed) to coarsen the microstructure (and thereby reduce grain boundary density) while keeping overall composition constant.
generation.conditions: Expose both sets to elevated temperatures (e.g., around 900°C) for prolonged durations (e.g., ~100 hours) in environments with controlled oxidizing atmospheres (e.g., pure O2 or ambient air) and reducing gas mixtures (e.g., H2-containing atmospheres).
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary density and the resulting microstructural features that control oxygen diffusion paths and the resulting oxide scale architecture.
generation.mechanism: The high density of grain boundaries inherent to the AM process serves as fast diffusion paths for oxygen, leading to preferential oxidation of Al and Cr that form an inner protective phase (Al2O3/Cr2O3). However, owing to the localized, accelerated oxidation at boundaries, the oxide scale develops a nonuniform, layered structure with an outer less-protective spinel-type phase that is prone to spallation. Under reducing environments, the equilibrium between oxidation and partial oxide reduction results in altered scale stability, further impairing long-term integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to post-annealed (coarser-grained) samples, the as-built high boundary density AM samples will exhibit faster initial mass gain, thinner or more discontinuous protective oxide layers, and higher susceptibility to scale spallation. Moreover, the oxide scale’s phase distribution (e.g., a distinct inner Al2O3/Cr2O3 layer versus an outer spinel region) will be more pronounced in the AM samples, and the degradation kinetics will be different under oxidizing versus reducing environments.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the degradation behavior (mass gain, oxide scale integrity, mechanical adhesion of the scale) of the as-built AM HEA under specified elevated temperature and controlled gas exposures.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies for temperatures approximately between 800°C and 1000°C and for exposure durations that permit diffusion-controlled oxidation (e.g., 100 hours); outside these conditions, other mechanisms (e.g., phase transformation or volatilization) may predominate.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis builds on combined findings: (a) the layered oxide formation and selective elemental oxidation seen in equiatomic HEAs (as discussed in PMC11169556, Results and Discussion) and (b) the influence of grain boundary density and microstructural refinement on oxidation kinetics observed in ultrafine-grained HEAs (PMC9026100). What is new here is the proposal that the unique AM-induced microstructure (with its high grain boundary density) specifically accelerates oxygen ingress along boundaries, altering protective scale formation in this non-equiatomic composition. Uncertainties include how the relatively lower Al content and the presence of Ti modify oxide chemistries compared to previously studied systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA samples: one as fabricated by additive manufacturing (retaining a high grain boundary density) and another set that is heat-treated post-fabrication to coarsen grains and reduce boundary density without altering composition. Expose both sets under identical conditions at 900°C in controlled oxidizing (e.g., pure O2) and reducing (e.g., 10% H2 in inert gas) atmospheres for 100 hours.
measurements: Mass gain or loss kinetics using thermogravimetric analysis
Oxide scale thickness, morphology, and phase distribution via SEM/TEM and XRD
Adhesion and spallation behavior via cyclic thermal and scratch testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the as-built samples (with high grain boundary density) do not exhibit significantly faster oxidation kinetics, more discontinuous or less adherent protective oxide layers, or if the oxide scale morphology and degradation behavior under oxidizing/reducing conditions are indistinguishable from the annealed, coarser-grained samples, then the hypothesis that grain-boundary-mediated oxygen diffusion governs the degradation mechanism is falsified.

AbstractThis work investigates the effect of ultrafine-grain microstructure on the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). The ultrafine-grain microstructure is obtained using stationary friction processing performed at two different rotational speeds, 400 and 1800 rpm, for 5 min duration. Processed samples demonstrate high depth of refinement (DOR) and ultrafine grain size (0.43–1 μm) at high rotational speeds along with significant phase transformations from BCC/B2 to FCC microstructure. Further, surface free energy of the ultrafine-grain microstructure is enhanced up to 35%. Oxidation kinetics of the ultrafine-grained sample is decelerated up to 12–48% in a temperature range of 850–1050 °C for a duration of 100 h. Chromia and alumina were the predominant oxides formed in almost all the samples oxidized at elevated temperature. In addition, spinel Co(Cr,Fe)2O4/Fe(Co,Cr)2O4 formation is also detected in the unprocessed oxidized samples. Processed samples rich in grain boundaries (GBs) promote internal oxidation to form Al-rich inner oxides. We used Cellular Automata to simulate the oxidation behavior of an AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy for a given set of rules. The simulation results match the experimental findings reported in the literature to a reasonable extent, suggesting that we have indeed captured a significant amount of the underlying physics of the process. The key findings may be summarized as follows: The primary goal of the single-crystal equimolar simulations was to isolate and understand the effect of alloy chemistry. Experimental alloys are, of course, more complex—but the approach adopted is to understand the effect of composition in isolation and then progress toward modeling of multi-phase microstructures. For the equimolar alloy, Al and Cr form the passivating oxides, and the concentration of α-Al2O3 and Cr2O3 grows over time in the oxide scale before approaching a steady state. The other oxides (namely those of Fe, Co, and Ni) form initially in larger concentrations, but their concentration in the oxide scale decreases with time.
